name: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone
lead: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH, also thyroliberin; the pharmaceutical form is protirelin) is a tripeptide, pyroglutamyl-histidyl-proline amide, made mainly by neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus. It stimulates the pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and prolactin, and so sits at the top of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis.[11][12]

TRH was the first hypothalamic releasing hormone to be structurally identified, in 1969, and its discoverers shared the 1977 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.[11] Beyond its endocrine role it acts in the brain, where it has been studied for effects on wakefulness, seizures, mood and neurological disease.[11] Clinical use has been mainly diagnostic, and trials of TRH for other conditions have been small or inconclusive. No source reviewed documents an established appearance-related use.

paras: TRH is cleaved from a larger precursor protein, and its pyroglutamyl and amidated ends protect it from some peptidases. It is rapidly degraded in blood, with a half-life of roughly five to six minutes.[11][12] Released into the portal circulation of the pituitary, it binds G protein-coupled receptors on thyrotroph cells, prompting TSH release, which in turn drives thyroid hormone production; thyroid hormones feed back to restrain TRH.[11][12]

TRH and its receptors also occur elsewhere in the nervous system and gut. Experimental work reports that TRH excites histamine-producing neurons that regulate arousal, and that it modulates glutamate release in brain tissue.[8][9]

The TRH stimulation test was historically used to distinguish hypothalamic from pituitary causes of hypothyroidism, a role largely replaced by ultrasensitive TSH assays.[11] Wikipedia also notes use in Japan-style indications such as spinocerebellar degeneration and disturbances of consciousness, and research interest in epilepsy, central nervous system injury and depression.[11]
Animal work has tested delivery methods intended to prolong TRH's brief action in the brain, including nanoparticles and implantable polymer discs, in seizure models.[2][4]

Wikipedia lists nausea, flushing, urinary urgency and a mild rise in blood pressure after intravenous administration, and tremor, sweating, shivering and restlessness after intrathecal administration.[11] A double-blind study in depressed alcoholic men reported mild and infrequent subjective side effects and no cardiovascular effects.[1]

Human studies of TRH are mostly old and small. A 1979 double-blind, placebo-controlled study in depressed alcoholic men found a beneficial behavioural effect three hours after injection, but not on later days.[1] A 1979 study of 17 schizophrenic patients reported a prompt decrease in psychotic symptoms of about half after intravenous protirelin, which then tended to fade.[3] A preliminary report examined TRH for spinal muscular atrophy, and Wikipedia states efficacy in ALS and spinal muscular atrophy has not been shown.[5][11]

Registered trials include large antenatal TRH studies for preventing respiratory distress in preterm infants (NCT00004778, Phase 3, 1,090 participants; NCT00004840, 996 participants), a Phase 2 trial for cancer-related fatigue that was terminated (NCT00790296), and Phase 2 trials of a TRH analogue coded KPS-0373 in spinocerebellar degeneration.[13][14][15][16]

timeline.event: TRH structure determined and synthesised by Guillemin and Schally.[11]
Guillemin and Schally share the Nobel Prize for brain peptide hormones.[11]
Placebo-controlled studies of protirelin in depressed alcoholic men and in schizophrenia.[1][3]

card.summary: The hypothalamic hormone that tells the pituitary to make TSH; a brain-active peptide with only small, dated human studies outside diagnostics.
card.note: Short half-life; non-endocrine uses remain investigational.

quick.overview:
TRH is a three-amino-acid hormone made in the hypothalamus. It signals the pituitary to release TSH and prolactin, which control the thyroid.

It appears in recovery-category peptide lists because of brain effects seen in research, but human data beyond diagnostic testing are small and old.
quick.mechanism: TRH binds receptors on pituitary thyrotroph cells to trigger TSH release, and is cleared within minutes; in the brain it influences arousal and neurotransmitter release.[8][11]
quick.risks: Reported effects of injected TRH include nausea, flushing and a mild blood pressure rise.[11] Because it raises TSH and prolactin, endocrine effects are expected. It has not been established as a treatment for the conditions studied.
